newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gets boost from strong stocks and bonds.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gets boost from strong stocks and bonds.

text.p: The dollar surged against most major currencies Friday, boosted by a stock market rally and growing signs of strength in the domestic economy.
The dollar hit its highest level in 2-1/2 years against the Swiss franc and hit a fresh 45-month high against the Japanese yen.

The dollar rose as high as 116.70 yen and stood at 116.39 late in New York, up from 115.58 yen late Thursday. It advanced to 1.3633 Swiss francs before settling at 1.3590, well above 1.3465 late Thursday.
The dollar hit its highest level against the yen since 117.25 in April 1993 and its highest against the Swiss franc since 1.4090 in June 1994.
The dollar rose to 1.5667 German marks from 1.5430 marks.

Slumping stock and bond prices hurt the dollar Tuesday and Thursday, but the stock rally Friday created new demand for dollars as more investors flocked to own U.S. assets. The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 101.60 points to 6,544.09.
"The market was a little bit negative on the dollar, based on the risk to the downside on stocks," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerishe Landesbank Girozentrale, in New York.
Foreign investors were particularly eager to buy dollars, traders said, since investments based in other currencies appeared unappetizing.
"Everyone was jumping on the bandwagon, it wasn't just any one particular customer," said Kisoo Park, senior dealer at Bank of Boston.
Bond prices were up much of the day despite additional data suggesting robust economic activity could lead to higher U.S. interest rates.
The government said construction spending rose 1.9 percent in November after surprisingly strong reports on December manufacturing data and consumer confidence earlier in the week.
Early strength in bonds gave traders another thumbs-up to buy dollars.
The dollar rose above 116.40 yen, its 1996 high set on Dec. 31, as speculation mounted that Japanese investors would be aggressive buyers of Treasury bonds upon returning from vacation next week.
The yield on the 30-year Treasury ended unchanged at 6.74 percent, the highest since late October.
In 1996, a strong U.S. economy and high interest rates sucked investor capital out of Japan, which propelled the dollar 12 percent higher against the yen for the year.
"It's dollar-financial-asset love here," said Alfonso Alejo, foreign exchange manager at Sakura Bank in New York.
"It's foreigners buying dollars to buy those assets and the Japanese may be among them and they don't have to wait until Monday," he added.
In other trade, the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3704 from C$1.3761 on Thursday.
The British pound fell to $1.6865 from $1.6949.
